_description: Canned per-section text for this pack's own semantic audit report, keyed by section letter. Data, not code: scripts/fill_pack_semantic_report.py reads this file and assembles docs/.audit_semantic_report.json from it. It lives here rather than inside that script because behavior step 65 scans scripts/*.py for instructions naming a Windows-only entry point, and release narrative that mentions run_audit.cmd or the word 'throw' is not an instruction - it is prose about instructions. Step 65 fired three times on one physical line of that script, was right every time, and the answer is to stop putting prose where a code scanner reads it rather than to police the wording or exempt the file (WQ-469). Each letter holds a 'summary' string and an 'evidence' array of {type, ref} entries; the constraints those must satisfy are enforced by audit_code_checks.py --verify-semantic-report, not here.

A.summary: Reviewed test harness: run_audit_tests.bat runs behavior + system verify; tests/test_pack_audit.py covers engine smoke plus the machine-Improve gate and the generic layoutPolicy default. Behavior steps 27-28 cover agent context refresh and layout hygiene end to end. Step 27 asserts the paste line's copy properties - single line, ASCII, BOM-free, no stray whitespace, and identical to the copy embedded in the brief - and passes -NoClipboard so a suite run never reaches into the user's clipboard. Step 29 adds cross-version parity: a probe runs on both PowerShell hosts and must produce identical writer bytes and identical parsed JSON, and it fails if a second BOM-free writer, an inline UTF8Encoding($false) write, or a script without #Requires appears. -DualShell re-runs the whole suite on the other host (verified: both pass). Step 26 now runs a real redirected install and asserts the pack tree, rules and recorded canonical path land in the scratch destination while the profile's install record and mcp.json stay byte-identical; it hashes only those install-owned files, because stamping all of %USERPROFILE%\.cursor went flaky against the running editor's own writes. Step 5b also enumerates pack/docs against packMirror now - the same installed-once-then-stale trap that this step already covered for rules and skills had two maintainer docs in it, so an agent reading the installed copy could be told a shipped feature was never built. 2.22.6 extended the same enumeration to pack/scripts and all of pack/templates after finding bootstrap-project.ps1, doctor.ps1 and all nine project templates outside packMirror - incremental syncs would never have carried a later edit into the installed copy that bootstrap actually runs from.

The extracted copy resolves its own pack root, passes the full suite, installs to a redirected target, and bootstraps a project that reaches the semantic gate.

L.summary: Agent wiring OK: AGENTS.md references run_audit; pack skill only; legacy path strings limited to migration helpers. The agent-code-audit skill now requires a Section B layout pass, and agent-defaults-always.mdc carries the context-refresh trigger pointing at docs/AGENT_REFRESH.md. Every rule on disk is tracked in manifest packMirror/packToUser, and sync-project-rules.ps1 enumerates pack/rules rather than a hardcoded list, so a newly added rule reaches projects as well as profiles (behavior step 5b runs that sync for real). Reviewed the handoff documents against the code they describe and corrected seven stale or self-contradicting claims, including a feature documented as both shipped and unimplemented; the session document that carried those cites was retired in 2.22.65 and docs/WORK_QUEUE.md is the only status claim left, with docs/handoffs/SESSION.md as the session-now channel (2.22.68); the boundary between a pack-shipped profile rule and a rule the user added on one machine is written down rather than living in one script's logic. This cycle read all 12 pack/rules, 5 workspace rules, 5 tool entry templates and 3 skills end to end and compared them for duplicate and missing coverage. Three defects closed: generic-deep-task-execution.mdc and generic-agent-doc-hygiene.mdc named this repo's WQ ids, phase numbers and HANDOFF sections in rules that install into every project, and no rule mentioned docs/AGENT_SESSION_START.md although all five entry templates tell agents to read it on the first turn - now a Session start section in the always-on rule rather than a thirteenth file. The overlaps that scan documented are now closed rather than carried: behavior step 46 fails when a shipped rule names a WQ id, HANDOFF, a pack-only spec, a phase number or a section number outside a line scoped to the maintainer repo - it found 11 further leaks on its first run that reading had missed, all reworded, and it is proven to fire on a planted leak and stay quiet on a scoped line. Terminal hygiene now splits by job (always-on rule = the before/after sequence, skill = diagnosis, on-demand rule = builds that never wait on a prompt, each stating what it does not cover), and one audit trigger list lives in audit-protocol.mdc and is repeated verbatim by agent-defaults-always.mdc and this repo's audit.mdc. Rule advice is now checked as well as rule wording: behavior step 47 resolves every pack/-rooted path cited by a rule, skill or pack doc, and found ensure-work-completion.ps1 copying a handoffs README template that had never been written - both handoff templates now exist and are mirrored. Project-relative citations, changelogs and deliberately-absent files are out of scope by design, because a checker that reports correct docs gets muted. Bootstrapping a project to read that new template found the copier plain-copying it while the WORK_COMPLETION path beside it substituted placeholders, so every project would have received a README titled with a literal {{PROJECT_NAME}}; both paths now share the substitution and the BOM-free writer, and bootstrap smoke step 23 fails on any unsubstituted placeholder in generated output. Running every generator rather than reading it then found the pack breaking its own build-hygiene rule: 12 bare pause statements across 4 root .cmd launchers, missed by 47 behavior steps because each one calls the .ps1 underneath with -NoPause while the .cmd layer is what a human double-clicks and an agent runs. All gated behind BUILD_NOPAUSE, step 48 guards it, and bootstrap output across 6 stack/target combinations is otherwise clean - manifest matches disk, no placeholders, no BOM, no mojibake. Vocabulary is now one word: the pack had used two synonyms for the same act across 519 occurrences in 56 files, so HANDOVER_NEXT_AGENT.md became HANDOFF_NEXT_AGENT.md with every reference moved (manifest maintainerOnlyPaths, VERSION_SYNC scanFiles, export.ps1, AGENTS.md, freshness requiredReads) and no redirect stub, since a stub is the parallel-doc pattern doc hygiene forbids. Two matches were narrowed by hand because the surviving string is ambiguous - verify-complete-picture.ps1 and step 46's token table both had to become HANDOFF_NEXT_AGENT, as bare HANDOFF also matches the docs/handoffs convention rules are supposed to name. Step 49 keeps the retired synonym out of every text file except the changelog and the checker, and the decision is written down in pack/docs/AGENT_HANDOFFS.md rather than left in a chat log. Root cleanup followed from those definitions: four finished documents deleted with the checks that policed them, and the session handoff trimmed from 788 to about 470 lines because roughly 400 duplicated the changelog and had begun to contradict it (section numbers preserved, since verify-complete-picture reads '## 11.'). Two defects surfaced while doing it - install.ps1 SkipRelPaths matched exact files only, so a maintainerOnlyPaths folder entry did nothing and docs/handoffs would have shipped every work slice into every profile (step 26 now asserts folder exclusion and that it stops at the folder boundary), and this repo's own docs/handoffs/README.md still carried {{PROJECT_NAME}} from before the 2.22.50 substitution fix. The pack handoff transfer is now itself a handoff under docs/handoffs/active/, passing verify-agent-handoffs.ps1 - WQ-426 carries the one step no guard can perform from here, untracking the three machine-local files in the other machine's git index, since a rule that travels as source cannot rewrite an index it is not running against.

M.summary: Version aligned: `VERSION` 1.8.0 matches install manifest and the engine is 2.22.123; `pack/docs/AUDIT_SYSTEM_CHANGELOG.md` documents 2.22.123 (doc truth: the maintainer's fear was the design finding, and acting on it was the release. Authorizing the OpenCode install he added that he feared we were trading one host-specific design for another instead of building something that works on all engines -- and WQ-479 had named that rule without applying it. WQ-480 applies it in the three places it was not true: the decision list moved out of pack/templates/cursor/hooks/preapproved.json to .agent-control/policy.json, found by walking up the tree the way OpenCode discovers .opencode, because shared data inside one host folder becomes that host data; its patterns changed from regexes to globs, which is the load-bearing fix since a glob compiles to a regex losslessly and a regex does not compile to a glob at all; and the semantics moved into conformance.json vectors, because one policy file stops two adapters disagreeing about the data and does nothing about them disagreeing over which rule wins, so an adapter is finished when it passes the vectors rather than when it reads the policy. Verified by the host rather than from documentation: OpenCode 1.18.30 installed via winget SST.opencode, and debug agent build in a bootstrapped project resolves all 33 compiled rules with run_audit.cmd as allow and install.ps1 as ask. The wait paid for itself because neither documented schema was right -- current docs show a v1 permission object and a v2 per-agent permissions array while the binary resolves permission, pattern and action -- so a block written from the docs would have been a phantom control. Refuse compiles to ask and never deny, since refuse means this control has no opinion rather than the owner is locked out, and allow is emitted before refuse so the narrower rule binds last as the binary orders its own built-ins. Step 83 grew from 12 arms to 20 and now runs the hooks from a staged project tree instead of where they ship, so the upward policy walk is exercised rather than the fallback, and it was re-proven under its own mutation. Deliberately unshipped: the OpenCode plugin handback, which is TypeScript with no JavaScript runtime on this host and needs provider credentials to fire, so it could be shown to load but never to fire -- and WQ-476 set the bar at proving a hook fires), 2.22.122 (doc truth: two maintainer questions found real gaps rather than session failures. WQ-478: nothing in this engine asked how work should be shaped, only whether enough of it was done -- he measured that batching beat concurrency on a list that ran over a week, and all fourteen prior always-on rules asked 'did you do enough' while none asked 'what is the cheapest correct way', so exhaustive serial work was the predictable output because an agent optimizes for what is checked. Parallelism is visible and batching is not, because the repeated cost is usually the gate rather than the work -- the guard prover costs a full suite run per entry. Shipped as the fifteenth always-on rule, with the clause that batching changes the shape and never the amount. WQ-479: the pack is tool-neutral everywhere except its newest controls, and the offload control was built against one editor's hook surface without asking whether the mechanism ports -- it does, but by luck, because the decision list is host-neutral JSON and only the plumbing is Cursor-specific. OpenCode turns out better provisioned than Cursor on both capabilities that matter here: a global rules path that actually loads, and declarative command pre-approval. `-Targets OpenCode` ships; the permission block and plugin handback deliberately do not, because no OpenCode here can verify them and an unverified config is a phantom control) and 2.22.121 (WQ-477 closed the case where the record itself kept regenerating a question the owner had answered three times -- publish requires StarterPack-Airlock on the host Desktop (WQ-465, decided), while `docs/WORK_QUEUE.md` recorded it as 'publish recorded as an open user decision', so every agent re-derived the ask correctly from the file. Three restatements in chat cannot outvote one line in a file, because a new session reads the file and not the history: a settled decision recorded as an open one is not a stale note, it is an instruction to ask again. Second cause recorded for the shape: the rule that used to carry the decision was deleted when its premise was retired, and retiring a premise is not retiring the content. Fixed by correcting the record and then, because a paragraph telling agents not to ask is what already failed, extending the WQ-476 control with a `settled` list that flags an ask re-raising one and cites where the decision is recorded -- checked before the command list and outside the refuse skip, since 'this is the human's call' is the exact framing that produced the defect) and 2.22.120 (WQ-476 closed the one rule in this pack that had no mechanism, and closed it by execution rather than by rewording it a fourth time -- the offload rule was present, loaded and correctly worded, violated across four sessions, and closed three times with better prose, because a sentence promising compliance is a status field and a status field cannot hold a proof. Which event does what was measured rather than inferred: `afterAgentResponse` carries the assistant's message in `text` and fires ~560ms before `stop`, while `stop` carries `status`, `loop_count` and `transcript_path` and no text, so the event that can see is not the event that can act and detection had to split from action. A violation is defined by a list rather than a judgement -- the ask section naming a command `preapproved.json` already clears the agent to run -- with both hooks reading one file so the approver and the detector cannot drift. Pre-approval ships available and unregistered because widening unattended execution is a project owner's call, and step 83 asserts that asymmetry. Step 83 runs the hooks with BOM-prefixed payloads instead of reading them, since the first live hook was installed, logging and approving nothing because Cursor prefixes its payload with a UTF-8 BOM) and 2.22.119 (a step guarding the bash wrappers failed with a message about a null `Path` and was right to fail but could not say so -- step 54 built its candidate list with `Join-Path` over three environment roots, one of which was empty on this shell, and the `if (-not $cand) { continue }` guard written to tolerate a missing candidate could never run because `Join-Path` throws while the array is still being built; guarding a result cannot protect against an input, and the inputs are now guarded per candidate. Recorded beside it: two red steps in one gate run were two causes, not one -- step 61 was the new WQ-476 hook writing `Set-Content -Encoding UTF8`, and fixing it does not touch step 54) and 2.22.118 (WQ-467 closed the only way an unreproducible event honestly can, which is that the forensics came back negative and the next occurrence is now detectable. Three rows in the control registry went from exempt to full mutation specifications inside an hour with no edit anyone could account for, the maintainer's own edits covering five rows of eight. The specifications were sound and all three were later proven by execution, so what was unexplained was never the content; it was the transition, and nothing in the system disagreed with it. Every writer is ruled out by reading it rather than by assuming: no script in this repository writes the source registry, the audit sync writes back into the source only under its pull switch, which was never passed, the mutation runner applies every specification to its own copy and reads the source registry with a plain read, and a sweep for writes anywhere under the audit folder finds only probe roots, with the real manifest read as a copy source. That leaves a human, an agent, or an editor buffer flushing over the file, and none of those is reproducible a day later. So the deliverable is detection, because the row's own re-open trigger was a second unexplained status change and nothing was watching for one. The exempt rows are now declared as a list in the registry and compared against the rows in both directions. The coverage step already printed the totals every run, and a printed count nobody recorded is a number rather than a check, which is precisely how the first transition passed as scenery. The list names steps rather than counting them, because a count cannot see a swap: one row retrofitted while another regresses to exempt leaves the total intact. The benign direction fails too, since a row that gained a proof without the declaration being updated is how a declaration rots into a number nobody trusts, which is the state this one was found in. The practical effect is that a status change must be edited in two places in the same change, and that second edit is the explanation the incident lacked. The printed line now names the exempt row rather than counting it, so a run says which row carries the debt. Three new in-process fixtures cover a row that stopped being exempt without the declaration changing, a row exempt without being declared, and a registry with no declaration at all; the coverage step keeps its registered mutation and was re-proven red under it on a quiet tree, baseline green and no collateral. Previously WQ-469 closed, so this narrative is no longer inside the script that assembles this report. The instruction scanner reads the two script folders for strings telling a reader to run a Windows-only entry point, and it fired three times on one physical line of the filler script, a line of 88,997 characters of canned audit prose. Every hit was correct on its own terms: the line named an entry point, later gained the word for raising an exception, and once carried the fix-switch spelling inside the very phrase describing the forbidden behaviour, because the match operator ignores case. A scanner cannot tell prose about an instruction from an instruction, and exempting the file was ruled out by the scanner's own comment, since that is how the next real offender gets in beside a tolerated one. Three hits on one line also showed the compounding shape, in that new prose inherits every literal already sitting on that line. The canned text now lives in a JSON data file beside the script, the script is a loader, and the move was verified by equivalence rather than by inspection: the report generated afterwards is identical to the one generated before it, field for field, with only the timestamp differing. Two findings fell out of the move. The manifest carried a small lie, in that the filler script was a declared consumer of the machine-local and maintainer-only path lists and read neither, because the consumer step counts a text mention of a key as reading it and the mentions were narrative; both declarations are gone, and the two distribution channels that must honour those lists still do. The general form is worth keeping, which is that prose in a scanned file does not only trip scanners, it satisfies them, and a registry entry created by a sentence is worse than a missing one because it reads as a verified fact. A new arm on the scanner step stops the prose returning, by refusing any line in the scanned set over 600 characters, a threshold the measurement makes uncontroversial since the longest line left anywhere in that set is 239. It joins the existing step rather than arriving as a new one because the subject is identical, namely what those files may contain, and that step was re-proven red under its registered mutation after the arms changed. Previously WQ-472 closed, so a marked failure line in this pack now means a real failure, and a run that exits zero while printing one fails the audit by itself. The suite runs child verifies against deliberately broken fixtures on purpose, since that is how a guard is shown to be able to fail, so those children report findings that are not findings. One arm tried to discard its child's output with an error-only redirect, which cannot touch the information stream every verify here writes on, so it captured nothing and discarded nothing: the finding printed to the host, the parent quoted it into its own report exactly as designed, and a certification run named a session-handoff path that exists in no file in this checkout. It cost a full diagnosis pass, because the file was clean, the child verify exited zero against it, and the suite reported no failures at all. The repair is an invariant rather than a patched arm, and it belongs to the parent, which is the one layer that sees both the exit code and everything the child wrote: the system verify now tees the suite's output instead of passing it straight through, and asks a tested helper whether a successful run printed anything marked as a failure. Teeing rather than capturing and re-printing matters, because the suite runs for minutes and a human watching it is entitled to see the steps as they go. Only failure markers count, since warnings and skips are things a passing run is expected to say. Suppressing the child would satisfy the same invariant and was the one repair ruled out, that being the earlier defect in the other direction, where a failing child that said nothing cost four audit runs and two disproven theories; so the arm captures all streams instead, which serves both halves at once, keeping the host quiet on a green run and finally giving the arm text to assert on rather than an exit code. That arm gained two assertions on the way past: the rejection must name the absolute path it found, and the accepting run must say it judged the roots. The new step tests the helper on fixtures rather than inferring it from its caller, the same shape an earlier step uses for the reason-quoting helper and for the same cause, since the parent that enforces the invariant cannot be run from inside the suite it runs. Three arms cover the sides an exit-code gate can get wrong, being a clean pass, a passing leak and a real failure; one covers a single captured string with a blank line in it, and two ask whether the parent still keeps a copy of the output and still calls the helper. A sixth arm scans this suite's own source for in-process script calls paired with an error-only redirect, because the invariant only fires once a leak exists while the scan fires when one is written. The population was measured before the invariant was turned on: with that one arm repaired, a green suite prints no marked failure lines at all, so one arm was the whole population rather than a sample of it. Proof: both affected steps red under their own mutations, one lane, baseline green, runner exiting zero, no collateral. The new step's mutation inverts the helper's exit-code gate so the leak detector goes quiet exactly where a leak can happen, and it reddens two arms rather than one. Reproducing the original incident by restoring the old redirect was rejected as the mutation, because no step runs the system verify against this suite, one step passing the skip switch and another existing to keep that recursion out, so only the source scan would have caught it and a mutation proven by a scan is weaker than one proven by behaviour. Previously WQ-471 closed, so the five guards that asserted only a zero exit now assert what was produced, and all five were re-proven on the changed arms. An earlier sweep looked for steps asserting that a child failed without asserting which finding produced the failure and fixed eleven of them; the mirror image was never swept, meaning steps whose only assertion is that a child succeeded, and it kept surfacing on its own three times while a different step was being proven, which is the argument for sweeping rather than waiting for a fourth. The portable export step was the worst of them, one exit code for the whole step with the output discarded, so a detector that had stopped comparing anything would have satisfied it, and the file it guards is the paste-at-session-start rules export for every tool that is not Cursor, a population that cannot notice staleness any other way since they read what the file says rather than what the pack ships. It now requires the verify to name the rules export it judged and to have compared this repository's own loaded rules, because that arm skips silently where the editor rules folder is absent and here it must run, and it carries the positive control it never had: a disposable two-file pack with exports generated into it and four kinds of drift planted in turn, a hand-edited export, a deleted one, a stale skill mirror and a loaded rule diverging from the pack source, each of which must be named, from a freshly synced export each time so one plant cannot be proven by another's damage. The hub-repair step shows the shape most clearly, because its first arm reads the tree and its second asserted a zero exit, and under that step's own mutation the second arm reports that the export matches the pack while the file is not on disk; it now requires the verify to name the export it judged, and a second control deletes that export again and requires the rejection to name it, so the case the repair exists for is the case the verify is proven to see. The portable bootstrap step asserted two zero exits and read nothing, so a bootstrap that generated nothing and a verify that judged nothing both passed, and it now reads the instructions hub, the rules export and the bootstrap record, and requires the verify to state the portable-only profile it was asked to enforce. The product-truth skip arm claimed the pack repository skips overlay checks while reading only a zero exit, and a skip and a full pass share that code, so it now requires the script to say it skipped. The work-completion delegation step could not be fixed by asserting output at all, and that reason generalises: the script it drives delegates without passing output through, so the child prints to the host and never reaches a captured stream, and the first attempt at the fix failed on exactly that. What discriminates is the verdict, so the control is a project that must fail the completion check, a roadmap still marking a shipped work item as next, because a delegation that has stopped happening cannot report a failure; the old arm's success line claimed the step had run, which the arm never checked. Evidence: the behavior suite reports zero failures after the rewrite, and the re-proof ran in two lanes with a green baseline inside each, five of five red under their own mutations and the runner exiting zero in both. One collateral record moved from suspected to confirmed, since the export mutation also fails the generated-project step, which drives a project through its own audit and therefore through the same verify, while the export step's earlier appearance in that list was contention rather than collateral. Previously WQ-433 closed, so a path under docs, scripts or tests named by a rule or a skill or a pack doc now has a declared owner, and the ones this pack delivers are checked for still being deliverable. Step 47 resolves only the cites rooted in the pack folder, which is why a design-reference doc that was cited but absent survived until a manual sweep, and the other three roots were left out for a good reason rather than an oversight, since a doc naming a project roadmap is describing the reader's project and this pack has none by decision. Measured before designing anything, an indiscriminate pass over those roots reports 68 findings on a clean tree and every one of them is correct advice about somebody else's tree, which is how the first attempt at this check got muted, and a muted check is worse than none. So the work was ownership rather than scanning, because a cite under those roots has three possible owners and only one of them is settled by asking whether the file is here. The first is this checkout, and that is the default for anything undeclared, so a new cite is checked without anyone listing it. The second is delivered, meaning the reader's project gets it from this pack, where existence here is the wrong question and the right one is whether the pack can still produce it, which is a stronger check because advice to keep a file no template writes is undeliverable; there are fourteen of those, each declared with its deliverer, including the one Python-stack file the bootstrap copies out of the pack scripts folder rather than templating. The third is the reader's own, cited as or equivalent, where nothing here can check it and the only honest treatment is to say so, so there are three of those, each carrying a reason, printed as information on every suite run, because an enumerated mute is the alternative to a quieter check. Ownership is declared per path rather than guessed from the citing file, because one paragraph cites both trees: the onboarding doc contrasts this repo's work queue with a bootstrapped app's roadmap in a single sentence. A negation filter fares no better, since that same doc says there is no session-start brief here, which a filter reads as an exemption and a reader reads as the truth. The declaration lives in the audit manifest, and a declaration nothing cites any more is a failure rather than a leftover, on the same reasoning as a find that matches zero times. New behavior step 81 carries it, mutation-proven, and it found a defect in itself on its first run: the extraction bound a string array parameter without allowing an empty string, so every document with a blank line failed to bind and the scan reported nothing, which is the shape of failure this pack keeps relearning, where a clean result and a blinded check are indistinguishable. It was caught by the arm that requires at least a hundred cites before believing a clean verdict, which is the same argument step 80 shipped a fixture for, and the lesson is now in the plan document as a floor on what a scan found. The step splits three ways: extraction tested in memory, where a backslash cite is the same path and a template extension must not truncate to the extension inside it and a pack-rooted cite belongs to step 47; judgement tested against a synthetic tree with six planted defects including a stale exemption; and the live surface. The mutation renames a cite in the rules-and-verify map and leaves the old one pointing at nothing, which is the original incident, and it reddens the undeclared default, which is the arm that matters. Deleting a template to exercise the deliverable arm was rejected because the bootstrap copies it, so four steps would have gone red and four failing steps prove less than one.
